title: All in His creation
hook: the good and the lost are all within His play

segments.voice: Yesterday, many millions: worshippers, pilgrims, poets, counted with wonder. Your line: millions, all His. Today the count keeps going, into harder territory. Day four hundred seventy-six, the end of a week.

Yesterday's list was easy to love. Pilgrims. Poets. Meditators. If the stanza had stopped there, it would be a nice hymn about good people. It doesn't stop there. The second stanza keeps the same drumbeat, kaee kot, many millions, and turns it on everyone we'd rather leave out of the picture. The proud. The cruel. The thieves. The gossips. The ones chasing money until they drop. It's the kind of list you'd expect before a sermon about who's going to be punished. And that sermon never comes.
screen: `YESTERDAY'S LIST WAS EASY.` → `NOW THE PROUD, THE CRUEL.` → `THE SERMON NEVER COMES.`

segments.voice: The second stanza goes: many millions are proud. Many millions are blind and ignorant. Many millions are misers, hard of heart. Many millions are cold inside, without feeling. Many millions steal what belongs to others. Many millions slander others. Many millions toil for wealth. Many millions wander in foreign lands. Then the turn, addressed straight to God: whatever You attach them to, to that they are attached. And the last line: Nanak, only the Creator knows His own creation. That's it. No verdict. Nobody's sentenced. The stanza simply says: these too are in the creation, and the One who made it is the only one who truly knows it. That doesn't mean Sikh teaching shrugs at cruelty or theft. The Gurus spoke hard words against oppression and greed, and Sikhs are asked to stand up for those who are wronged. But this stanza is about something else: the urge to stand outside the creation and sort it into the saved and the lost, as if we were the one who made it. Kartaa is the word for the Creator, the Doer. Only the Kartaa knows the creation. All of it is within His play. That's humbling, and it's also oddly freeing. You don't have to be everybody's judge today. And this is where the week ends. Seven days ago, the true aparas. Then pandit, nihkaram, Singh and Kaur and the badge set down. Then the crowd: so many, many millions, and today, all of them, in the play.
screen: `THE PROUD, THE CRUEL, THE THIEVES.` · `WHATEVER YOU ATTACH THEM TO.` · `ONLY THE CREATOR KNOWS IT.` · `NOT EVERYBODY'S JUDGE.` · then, large: `ALL IN THE PLAY.`

segments.voice: The practice: judge no one today. Begin now. Bring to mind someone you've been judging lately. A relative, a politician, a coworker, a stranger online. Don't argue with your judgment or pretend they're right. Just picture them inside the same creation as you, held by the same hands. Breathe in: they're in the play. Breathe out: so am I. You can still disagree. You can still say no. You're just setting down the gavel for one day. The bell holds the time.
Kartaa, the Creator, the Doer. The proud and the lost, the cruel and the kind, many millions, all within His play; only the Kartaa knows it.
Your line: all in the play. Today, when you feel the gavel coming down on someone, set it down for one breath. Day four hundred seventy-six. A week, done.

screen: `DAY 476 COUNTS.` → `A WEEK OF TRUE NAMES AND MANY MILLIONS.` → `TOMORROW: LIVING ASHTPADI 10.`

howItsDone: Sikhs read this stanza of Sukhmani Sahib as a reminder that only the Creator knows the creation, while still standing against injustice as the Gurus taught.

original.note: Gurmukhi: kartaa, the Creator, the Doer; ashtpadi ten says only the Kartaa knows the creation.

trapdoor: what you thought: all in the play means nothing matters.
what it means: everyone is within the creation, and only the Creator knows it, so we aren't its judges.
what a scholar hears: 'jit jit laavahu tit tit lagnaa' (whatever You attach them to) frames human paths within hukam; Sikh thought pairs this with active resistance to injustice.

sources.work: Guru Granth Sahib (Guru Arjan, Gauri Sukhmani)
